## Short version

A TLB (translation lookaside buffer) is a small cache in the CPU that stores recent translations from virtual addresses to physical addresses. On a big-memory server this cache covers a very small share of the memory, and each miss costs up to 4 extra memory reads. Huge pages make each TLB entry cover at least 512 times more memory, and the main risks are allocation stalls, higher memory use, and reserved memory that nothing else can use.

Assumption: x86-64 Linux.

## Words used here

- **Page**: the unit in which the operating system maps memory. The default size is 4 KiB.
- **Page table**: the in-memory tree that maps each virtual page to a physical page. It has 4 levels on x86-64.
- **Page walk**: the CPU reading that tree after a TLB miss, one memory read per level.
- **Huge page**: a page of 2 MiB or 1 GiB instead of 4 KiB.
- **THP** (transparent huge pages): the Linux feature that gives a program 2 MiB pages automatically.
- **hugetlbfs**: the Linux feature where the administrator reserves a fixed pool of huge pages and programs request them explicitly.
- **khugepaged**: the kernel thread that merges 4 KiB pages into 2 MiB pages in the background.
- **Compaction**: the kernel moving pages to create one contiguous free block.
- **NUMA node**: one CPU socket together with the memory attached to it.
- **RSS** (resident set size): the physical memory a process currently holds.

## 1. What a TLB is

Programs use virtual addresses, and memory chips use physical addresses. The CPU translates on every memory access. The TLB holds the most recent translations, one entry per page.

```
virtual addr --> [ TLB ] --hit--> physical addr  (no extra read)
                    |
                   miss
                    v
          [ page walk: up to 4 memory reads ] --> fill TLB
```

A recent Intel server core has about 2,000 entries in its second-level TLB (est., the count depends on the CPU model) [Intel Optimization Reference Manual, TLB parameter tables].

## 2. Why misses are expensive on a big-memory server

Example: a 512 GiB server and a TLB with 2,048 entries (est.).

| Page size | Memory covered by the TLB | Last-level page tables for 512 GiB | Reads per walk |
|---|---|---|---|
| 4 KiB | 8 MiB (0.0015% of memory) | 1 GiB | 4 |
| 2 MiB | 4 GiB (0.78% of memory) | 2 MiB | 3 |
| 1 GiB | CPU-dependent (see section 4) | 4 KiB | 2 |

- **Coverage shrinks.** The TLB size is fixed, but memory size grows. A program that reads a large heap in random order misses the TLB on most accesses.
- **The tables do not fit in the CPU caches.** 1 GiB of last-level tables is larger than the caches (tens to a few hundred MiB). The last read of a walk then goes to main memory. One such read costs est. 100 ns (about 300 cycles at 3 GHz).
- **Upper levels are cached.** The CPU keeps a separate cache for the upper levels of the tree [Intel SDM Vol. 3A, section 4.10.3]. A typical miss therefore costs one slow read, not four.
- **Virtual machines multiply the cost.** Both the guest and the host translate addresses. One miss can need up to 24 memory reads [Bhargava et al., ASPLOS 2008].
- **Measured size of the problem.** Databases, in-memory caches, and graph analytics spent up to 10% of execution cycles on TLB misses [Basu et al., "Efficient Virtual Memory for Big Memory Servers", ISCA 2013].

## 3. How huge pages help

L4 to L1 are the four levels of the page table.

```
4 KiB page:  L4 --> L3 --> L2 --> L1 --> data   (4 reads)
2 MiB page:  L4 --> L3 --> L2 ---------> data   (3 reads)
1 GiB page:  L4 --> L3 ----------------> data   (2 reads)
```

- **More coverage.** One entry covers 2 MiB, which is 512 times more than 4 KiB.
- **Shorter walk.** The walk stops one or two levels earlier.
- **Smaller tables.** 512 GiB needs 2 MiB of last-level tables, which fits in the CPU cache.
- **Cheaper misses.** A workload that touches more than 4 GiB at random still misses the TLB. Each miss then reads from the CPU cache, not from main memory.
- **Fewer page faults.** One fault maps 2 MiB, so first use of memory causes 512 times fewer faults.

Linux offers two mechanisms:

| | THP | hugetlbfs |
|---|---|---|
| Page sizes | 2 MiB | 2 MiB and 1 GiB |
| Who asks | Kernel decides, or program calls `madvise` | Program asks explicitly |
| Memory reserved up front | No | Yes |
| When no huge page is free | Uses 4 KiB pages, no error | `mmap` fails, or the process is killed |

## 4. What can go wrong

**With THP**

- **Stalls inside page faults.** The kernel may run compaction during a fault, and the faulting thread waits for it. The `defrag` setting controls this [Linux `Documentation/admin-guide/mm/transhuge.rst`]. `compact_stall` in `/proc/vmstat` counts these events.
- **Memory use grows.** A program that touches 1 byte receives 2 MiB. khugepaged merges a 2 MiB range even when 511 of its 512 small pages were unused (default `max_ptes_none=511`) [transhuge.rst]. RSS can grow until the kernel kills the process [Kwon et al., "Ingens", OSDI 2016].
- **Coverage varies between runs.** After long uptime, free memory is fragmented. The kernel then uses 4 KiB pages without an error. Performance differs between a fresh boot and a machine that has run for weeks. `thp_fault_fallback` in `/proc/vmstat` counts these cases.
- **Pages get split.** A partial `munmap`, `mprotect`, or `madvise` on a 2 MiB range splits it back into 4 KiB pages. Swapping does the same. The gain disappears without a message.

**With hugetlbfs**

- **Pool too large.** Reserved pages cannot be swapped or used for file cache. The rest of the system can run out of memory while pool pages are free.
- **Pool too small.** `mmap` fails with `ENOMEM`, or the process receives `SIGBUS` on first touch [Linux `Documentation/admin-guide/mm/hugetlbpage.rst`].
- **Per-node pools.** The pool is divided across NUMA nodes. A process bound to one node can exhaust that node's pool while other nodes have free pages.
- **1 GiB pages need boot-time reservation.** After boot the kernel rarely finds 1 GiB of contiguous free memory.
- **Few 1 GiB TLB entries on some CPUs.** Skylake-generation cores have 16 second-level entries for 1 GiB pages, which cover 16 GiB [Intel Optimization Reference Manual]. On such a CPU, 1 GiB pages can perform worse than 2 MiB pages.

**With both**

- **Longer single faults.** The kernel clears a page before first use. Clearing 2 MiB takes est. 0.2 ms, and clearing 1 GiB takes est. 100 ms (both assume a clear rate of 10 GiB/s). Touching all memory at startup moves this cost out of the request path.
- **fork and copy-on-write.** After `fork`, the first write to a shared hugetlbfs page copies the full huge page. With THP, newer kernels split the page into 4 KiB pages, and older kernels copied the full 2 MiB. Redis documents latency spikes from this [Redis docs, "Diagnosing latency issues"].
- **No gain.** A workload whose active memory already fits in the TLB coverage gains about nothing.

## 5. What to measure before the review

```
# Current settings. Many distributions already enable THP.
cat /sys/kernel/mm/transparent_hugepage/enabled
cat /sys/kernel/mm/transparent_hugepage/defrag
grep -i huge /proc/meminfo

# TLB entry counts of this CPU, per page size
cpuid -1 | grep -i tlb

# Share of CPU cycles spent in page walks (Intel event names)
perf stat -p <pid> \
  -e cycles,dtlb_load_misses.walk_active \
  -e dtlb_store_misses.walk_active,itlb_misses.walk_active \
  -- sleep 30

# After enabling: are huge pages really in use?
grep -E 'thp_fault_alloc|thp_fault_fallback|compact_stall' /proc/vmstat
grep AnonHugePages /proc/<pid>/smaps_rollup
```

- The `walk_active` counters divided by `cycles` give the share of time spent in page walks. That share is the approximate upper limit of the gain from huge pages.
- Event names differ between CPU models. `perf list | grep -i walk` shows the names on your machine.

Insufficient data: the gain for your workload. The page-walk cycle share from the `perf stat` command above resolves it.
